title: Over-regulating AI could kill productivity's golden goose
full_text:
Just when you imagined the burden of business regulation in Australia could not become heavier, along comes a new government regime to manage the roll out of artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres.
The new Office of Artificial Intelligence (OAI) will add to the one hundred or so existing regulators at the federal level - alongside dozens of others among the states - that risk making doing business in Australia even more complicated and expensive.
AI earning its "social license" is a woke way of saying interventionist government will seek to control outcomes.
There is much we don't yet know about the new regulator, but even more rules and red tape are coming our way.
The new regime will operate nationally, with all states territories involved, according to the speech the PM delivered in Sydney yesterday.
At the outset, let's be clear. The rapid roll out of AI affects all aspects of corporate and personal life.
Millions of people already embrace the benefits of AI. But many others are terrified about its potential impact on their lives and sustainability of their jobs.
There clearly is a need to set appropriate guardrails to make sure progress aligns with national interests.
But such guardrails should not be established to placate irrational fears of widespread job losses, because there is no so-called "jobs apocalypse" - at least not yet.
In fact, the government's own Department of Employment and Workplace reported this week that jobs in AI-exposed sectors of the economy grew in the just over three years between Chat GPT's emergence in late 2022 and February this year.
Yes, most jobs will change because of AI and some existing roles undoubtedly will be lost. But, on the evidence to hand, the roll out of AI is not nearly as disruptive to labour markets as some had feared.
In fact, many new jobs will emerge as the technology matures and its adoption spreads.
Many already have.
Context here matters. As we all well know now, Australia is suffering an extended crisis of productivity that is dragging down living standards.
Average productivity gains this decade are the worst in 60 years. There are many reasons for this, including the layer upon smothering layer of overbearing regulation that has introduced more complexity and cost.
Compliance with all these rules distracts decision makers from strategic and creative deliberations.
Last year, Mandala Partners found that more than half of board time already is consumed with compliance and regulation.
Much of it is unnecessary box-ticking. And now there will be more red tape applied to one of the fastest-growing areas of the economy.
There's no obvious sign of a much-needed improvement in our dismal productivity.
There's no realistic prospect of whole of system tax reform (instead, we are getting piecemeal tinkering) and there's zero chance of the recent productivity-killing re-regulation of workplace arrangements being reversed.
Much of our industry policy will continue to reward corporate failure. And, across many aspects of the economy, including on painfully slow approval times and more punitive taxation of capital, Australia is signaling to global capital allocators they'd be better off nesting their investments elsewhere.
The exception, of course, is the largely unexplored and unmeasured boost from AI. Even its strongest advocates cannot yet grasp what benefits can be achieved here.
AI looms as a golden goose for Australia's productivity that, at its worst, could mitigate our slide into global underperformance.
At best, AI's prudent adoption could super charge a turnaround in our dismal productivity.
But, while other countries, including the US, throw open their doors to AI and related investment in data centres, we erect barriers.
On AI, this seems to partly be aimed at placating shouty voices of entrenched dissenters and the technology luddites in organized labour, who mount spurious arguments about coming workplace wastelands. And we're likely to hear more of those from the upcoming ALP conference, but these claims are not supported by the evidence.
The emerging anecdotal evidence of the productivity benefits to be gained from AI are already pointing to gains in output relative to inputs of up to 80 per cent, all but overnight.
AI has quickly transformed thousands of workplaces, freeing up millions of workers from drudgery now undertaken by machines.
The explosive growth in data centres is the only thing supporting otherwise flaccid business investment and weak growth in our economy.
But data centres also are in the frame in the new regime. The government will legislate new requirements for use of energy and water, among other considerations about impacts on affected communities.
The enthusiasm with which the federal government has embraced regulating this new and potentially world-changing technology is demonstrated by the fact that the new regulator will be established within the Prime Minister's own department. It's gone straight to the top, albeit with oversight of relevant ministers and departments.
What the PM describes as adding "clarity" to global allocators of capital to many will be another layer of complexity and cost.
Overreach risks chilling investment that could end up elsewhere. Australia's high labour and energy costs already are impediments.
But we are a trusted partner, partly because of our predictable institutional systems. For now. There is time to get this new regulatory regime right.
National Cabinet will be asked to help shape the relevant legislation the government hopes to pass early next year.
Members should take their time and not jump at shadows. Unlike with the recent contentious tax measures, consultation with stakeholders before decisions are made will be critical.
Because the stakes here are too high. Golden geese do not fly our way often, especially in the form of well-timed landings amid a crisis.
We must be careful not to smother this particular bird in red tape before it has a chance to nest and proliferate.
*
Stephen Walters is a Senior Fellow at the Centre for Independent Studies.
